docs.title: Imperial Summons
docs.text:
Enter without ceremony

Officium Imperiale Praedarorum

A dispatch has arrived under the seal of the Imperial Throne.

V Break the Imperial Seal

Under the authority of the Imperial Throne

V

To the bearer of this notice,

By examination and sworn witness, it has been determined that your body retains mana beyond the measure required for ordinary life. Your name has therefore been entered into the Provisional Register of Praedari.

This distinction is rare. It is an honor, a responsibility, and a matter of Imperial interest.

You are hereby summoned to present yourself before the nearest Chartered Academy or appointed Imperial examiner. There, your capacity will be measured, your discipline observed, and the path of your education determined.

Until that assessment is complete, you are instructed neither to conceal your gift nor to demonstrate it without sanction. Bring this notice with you. Its seal is proof that the Throne has recognized what now stirs within you.

The Empire does not leave power untaught. It does not leave potential unused.

Come prepared to be tested. Come prepared to be changed. Come prepared to become more than nature first intended.

By mandate of the Throne,

The Office of Praedari Affairs

docs.title: Magic Item Classification
docs.text:
Valeria classifies magical items by the power and complexity of their enchantment and the mana development required to use them safely.

There are six classifications:

docs.title: Ordinarius
docs.text:
The lowest classification.

Its enchantment is completely self-contained and requires no personal mana. Anyone can use it if they understand how it operates.

docs.title: Insignis
docs.text:
More advanced than Ordinarius, but still completely self-contained.

It requires no Praedari training and can be used by ordinary people.

docs.title: Eximius
docs.text:
The first classification that requires mana from its wielder. The user must possess developed mana pathways and sufficient control to connect with the item.

Minimum Rank: Peritus

docs.title: Praestans
docs.text:
Requires greater mana reserves, stronger pathways, and better control than Eximius equipment.

Minimum Rank: Potens

docs.title: Singularis
docs.text:
Extremely advanced magical equipment that depends upon the wielder's mana density, stability, and resilience, not merely their ability to supply mana.

Minimum Rank: Excelsus

docs.title: Aeternus
docs.text:
The highest recognized classification. Aeternus items place extraordinary demands upon their wielder and represent the limits of magical craftsmanship.

Minimum Rank: Supremus

docs.title: Mana
docs.text:
Mana is the living force that makes the heart beat. It keeps blood flowing through the veins of the newborn and the old alike, unseen and unfelt by most people even as it passes through the air and sustains every living being.

Most creatures will live their entire lives without ever seeing or feeling mana enter their bodies. They may study it, understand that it exists, and witness what others can accomplish with it, yet mana itself will remain an alien concept to them. They know it is there only because the world has given them enough evidence to believe it.

But not everyone is born equal.

For a rare few, mana is less like an unseen force and more like an old companion. Every race possesses a different rate of mana attunement, with elves having the greatest natural chance of being born attuned. Those capable of sensing and using mana often grow beyond the ordinary limits of their bodies and minds. They may become stronger, faster, sharper in thought, or possess a presence difficult for others to ignore.

For those who can truly wield mana, the laws of nature are not absolute rules, but challenges to be overcome. A spell that can split the earth with a sweep of the hand. A sword that move faster than the naked eye can follow. A body becomes light enough to descend from a cliff with the ease of a falling feather.

People born with this gift have shaped civilizations throughout history. They become warriors, scholars, rulers, healers, explorers, and countless other things according to their own desires. Some believe that greater power brings greater responsibility, and spend their lives protecting others and leading their people towards a better future.

Others choose very different paths.

In the tongue of the Empire, those who can sense, retain, and wield mana are known as Praedari.

docs.title: Praedari
docs.text:
Praedari is a name bestowed through the common tongue of the Empire, a moniker given to people capable of retaining more than the minimum amount of mana required to sustain life. Across Avara, they are revered and feared by the masses, for even the weakest among them possesses something that most people will never experience for themselves.

A Praedari rarely blends completely into an ordinary crowd. There is often an unexplainable shift that follows them when they enter a room, something difficult to identify but equally difficult to ignore. Some carry this presence more strongly than others, and those familiar with Praedari eventually learn to recognize that something about the person before them is different.

The disciplines and ways of mana vary greatly from one Praedari to another. Talent, training, and personal preference shape what each individual eventually becomes. Some pursue speed until their movements surpass what the naked eye can follow, while others strengthen their bodies until ordinary weapons struggle to harm them. Others attune themselves to nature and the forces surrounding it, learning to bend laws of the universe that most people can only obey.

Individuals with such potential are rarely left entirely to their own devices. They must be trained and disciplined if they are to become the best versions of themselves and use their abilities for the betterment of society. A Praedari who receives no guidance may never reach their full potential. While one who possesses great power without discipline will eventually become a variable that must be removed.

There is no equality even among Praedari. Some are only slightly stronger than an ordinary person, remarkable enough to stand above the average citizen but hardly powerful enough to reshape the world around them. Then there are those who exist at the opposite extreme, individuals capable of destroying a village while taking a midnight stroll.

Imagine looking across an open field and seeing one such Praedari lying peacefully beneath the sun. He appears completely relaxed, enjoying the warmth and the breeze like any other person might, yet you know that with little more than a gesture he could level the village behind you. Nothing about the sight is immediately threatening until he notices you watching and turns his attention in your direction.

He smiles and raises a hand in greeting.

Perhaps the smile is genuine. Perhaps he means you no harm at all, but the uncertainty is enough to place an uncomfortable thought in your mind. The man waving pleasantly across the field possesses enough power to decide whether you, your family, and everyone in your village will live to see another sunrise. Knowing that someone holds such power will never sit comfortably in the mind of an ordinary person, no matter how kindly that person behaves.

To be born a Praedari is therefore to lose much of the certainty of an ordinary life. Power attracts attention, and attention brings expectations that cannot easily be escaped. Some will revere a Praedari for what they can accomplish, others will hate them for what they represent, and many will fear them simply because of what they might do.

What a Praedari becomes is ultimately their choice, but the world will respond to that choice in equal measure.

docs.title: Mana Reinforcement and Resistance
docs.text:
As a Praedari grows stronger, mana settles deeper into the body, reinforcing flesh, bone, and organs, against attacks with no magical property. Steel can still cut, bullets can still penetrate, and sufficient force can still kill, but the damage will not fully reach a praedari with strong foundation.

Among the rare and exceptional Praedari, this reinforcement develops into something greater. Their mana becomes dense enough to resist attacks directly, causing ordinary weapons to struggle to reach the flesh beneath.

Bullets flatten, explosion and fire will only give them warmth barely touching their clothes. To properly injure an Exceptional Praedari, an attack must carry mana. The stronger the Praedari, the more powerful the opposing mana must be to overcome their protection.

Against the strongest among them, Mana is not an advantage in a fight, it's mandatory for a chance to wound them.

docs.title: Praedari Ranks
docs.text: The empire divides Praedari into six ranks based on mana capacity, density, control, output, and overall development.

docs.title: Tiro
docs.text:
The lowest recognized rank. Most Tiro are first year academy students or newly discovered Praedari. Their mana is still immature, and their control remains incomplete.

They are considered potential rather than fully trained Praedari.

docs.title: Peritus
docs.text:
The first fully developed rank. A Peritus possesses reliable mana control and enough development to use their abilities consistently in ordinary work or combat. Most peristus do not become soldiers. Peristus can be seen scattered around the empire working in civilian professions such as agriculture, industrial production, medicines and many more. They are the foundation that supports the imperial army.

Many academy graduates or talented students enter the society at this rank.

docs.title: Potens
docs.text:
An experienced Praedari whose mana use has become largely instinctive. Potens are seasoned practitioners with greater reserves and control than Peritus. In the military, they form the core of Praedari units.

Most Potens are veterans that have built mountains of experience in their respective fields.

docs.title: Excelsus
docs.text:
An elite Praedari with significantly greater mana and exceptionally refined control. Many Praedari never progress beyond Potens. Those who reach Excelsus are uncommon and often become prominent within their profession. Excelsus also marks the minimum level of mana capable of reliably wounding Eminens and Supremus.

Within the military, they form the core of Elite Praedari units. Around half of all Excelsus in the empire serve within the military.

docs.title: Eminens
docs.text:
An exceptionally rare Praedari whose mana has developed true density. Their mana saturates the body so completely that ordinary weapons struggle to inflict any injuries. Mana of at least Excelsus level is normally required to reliably bypass this protection.

Most Eminens are cultivated with significant Imperial support and serve as major military assets.

docs.title: Supremus
docs.text:
The highest recognized Praedari rank. Their mana capacity, density, control, and output exceed even Eminens by a considerable margin. A Supremus can function as a military force in their own right and may be capable of confronting entire formations alone. They are extraordinarily rare and are usually tied to the Imperial Family, the Custodes Praetoriani, or other major Imperial institutions leaders.

Supremus has no defined upper limit. Two individuals may hold the same rank while possessing vastly different levels of power.

docs.title: Wizard
docs.text:
A Wizard concentrates mana around the mind, where memory, calculation, and understanding shape their magic. Rather than creating an effect entirely through mana, Wizards study the laws of nature and use mana to make a precise alteration that causes the desired result.

A small spark becomes fire, a fracture spreads through stone, or a shift in air becomes something far greater. Their spells are built from complex diagrams, symbols, calculations, and mana pathways recorded within spellbooks.

For combat, Wizards prepare these diagrams beforehand by repeatedly circulating mana through specific pathways beneath the skin until the body remembers them. These pathways eventually appear as faint geometric markings resembling an arcane tattoo, that activate when the spell is cast.

At higher levels, many wizards create their own personal spells, diagrams that could be understood only by the user. Many have tried to thread this path, only a few came out unscathed and succeeded.

Their strength lies in knowledge, preparation, and using mana to nudge nature to do the rest.

docs.title: Artificer
docs.text:
An Artificer's magic comes from the devices they create, not directly from their own body. Their unique talent allows them to understand and construct artificial pathways through which mana can flow. They incorporate these pathways into weapons, tools, armor, and machines, treating mana as simply another part of engineering alongside metal, heat, pressure, electricity, and motion.

When an Artificer produces a magical effect, the device itself becomes its point of origin. A thrown device releases its magic. The final form would be varied, depending on the intrinsic design of the user.

Their creations usually aren't made for just anyone either. An artificer's own mana is often woven into the device's workings, serving as both fuel and key.

Artificer is the backbone of science and inventions, many artificers have contributed to the progress of humanity. Some create new vehicles, new alchemic formulas and last but not least magic items.

The artificer ingenuity creates the device that allows them to impose their will on the law of nature itself.

docs.title: Sorcerer
docs.text:
A Sorcerer is born with an unusually close connection to mana, which gathers strongest around the heart and spreads through branching pathways across the body. These pathways function like a natural magical circuit. By moving their body, Sorcerers guide mana through those channels and draw surrounding mana into the spell..

Their casting is highly physical. Their movements resemble a series of traditional martial arts sets of movements. Unlike Wizards, Sorcerers do not rely on prepared diagrams. They can alter a spell while casting it, changing its range, direction, shape, speed, or intensity in the moment. With enough mastery, larger movements can be reduced to smaller gestures, though doing so requires greater concentration and control.

Much like Wizards, exceptional Sorcerers may create spells of their own. The difference is that they do not discover them through new formulas, but through new patterns of bodily performance and mana.

Only a tiny fraction of Sorcerers ever succeed in finding such a pattern. Those who do may produce a spell unlike anything anyone has seen before, born not from written theory, but from a way of shaping mana that only they discovered.

A Sorcerer's strength lies in instinctive control, flexibility, and shaping magic through the body itself.

docs.title: Druid
docs.text:
A Druid concentrates mana around the lungs, using breaths as the connection between their body and the living world. Rather than creating nature, they strengthen what already exists. Seeds, roots, spores, water, and other living material can be flooded with mana and forced to grow or change at unnatural speed.

Because of this, Druids often carry seeds, herbs, roots, spores, and other natural materials with them, giving them something to work with even where nature is scarce. Their magic relies heavily on breathing, understanding, and connection with nature itself. The same principle allows them to transform their own bodies, using mana to take on the form of creatures they deeply understand.

The path of the Druid is to learn from nature itself, yet even after millennia of study, nature continues to reveal things no one before them understood. A small number of Druids discover laws hidden within the natural world and learn to exploit those principles to create spells of their own, while others encounter beasts unknown to their predecessors and eventually learn to assume those forms themselves.

Many Druids have spent their lives searching for such discoveries, pushing deeper into nature in the hope of understanding something no one else has seen. Some succeed and return with knowledge that changes what other Druids believe possible. Others go too far, misunderstand what they have found, or simply reach for something they were never capable of mastering, and nature takes them as the price of trying.

A Druid's strength lies in learning and enhancing their connections to nature.

docs.title: Ranger
docs.text:
A Ranger concentrates most of their mana around the dantian, using it to reinforce the body, sharpen the senses, steady movement, and strengthen attacks. A smaller portion gathers around the lungs, giving them a limited connection to nature. Unlike Druids, Rangers do not fully devote themselves to the living world. They keep most of their mana focused on themselves.

Yet, a true Ranger's strength lies beyond combining physical enhancement with practical nature magic.

At a glance, Rangers may seem like underwhelming combinations of Druids and Fighters. That impression could not be further from the truth. A true Ranger does not rely on magic and physical strength alone, but learns to fight through nature itself, turning the terrain, its creatures, and its conditions into extensions of their own skill.

At higher Praedari ranks, Rangers can attune their mana so completely to a chosen environment that the boundary between hunter and terrain begins to blur. Their presence becomes extraordinarily difficult to detect, almost resembling the natural concealment of a Rogue, while every part of the surrounding land becomes something they can exploit. Fighting an accomplished Ranger within their chosen terrain borders on suicide, for there, nature itself becomes their blade.

Druids are the nurturers of nature. Rangers are its apex predators.

docs.title: Artist
docs.text:
An Artist concentrates mana around the head, focusing on the parts where memory, imagination, and emotion rest. This is how their magic manifests. An Artist's strength lies in emotion, expression, and resonance with the mana.

They do not cast through calculation. They cast through performance and emotional resonance. Music, painting, dance, poetry, storytelling, and other forms of art can all become mediums for magic.

Emotion is the true catalyst. The stronger and more genuine the feeling behind the performance, the more powerfully their mana responds and spreads through those who experience it.

At higher levels, the boundary between expression and reality can begin to blur, allowing an Artist’s work to produce effects that feel almost real. From that expression, something entirely new may be born into the world, whether beautiful, horrifying, or unlike anything that existed before it.

That freedom carries its own danger. Some Artists lose control of the mana sustaining their creations, and what began as an act of expression turns against its creator. In the worst cases, they are eventually swallowed whole by their own masterpieces.

docs.title: Warrior
docs.text:
A Warrior concentrates mana around the heart and uses it to drive the body far beyond its natural limits. In battle, they deliberately accelerate the heart, blood flow, and adrenaline response, forcing mana through muscle, bone, and tendon.

Every wound they receive becomes fuel to keep their heart at an accelerated state. This greatly increases their strength, endurance, pain tolerance, and durability. What appears to be uncontrolled rage is usually deliberate. A trained Warrior remains mentally focused while pushing their body into an extreme combat state.

Their fighting style favors overwhelming physical force and persistence. Every strike carries the weight of a mana-reinforced body, and once committed to an attack, a Warrior is exceptionally difficult to stop.

And yet a true Warrior understands that overwhelming physical force and sheer persistence are only the foundation. An exceptional Warrior learns to accelerate the body’s own regeneration, endure wounds that would cripple others, or concentrate everything they possess into a single final strike. There are many paths a Warrior can follow beyond the simple strengthening of the body.

In the end, a true warrior finds their own path.

docs.title: Fighter
docs.text:
A Fighter channels mana through the nervous system, shortening the gap between thought and movement. This gives them exceptional reaction speed, coordination, and control. Their bodies respond to subtle changes in an opponent's movement almost instinctively.

Fighters also learn weapons unusually quickly. The mana reinforce their muscle memory and techniques become deeply ingrained incomparably faster to normal humans. This allows Fighters to become a walking encyclopedia of martial arts from various weapons and disciplines.

At higher levels, they develop a personal combat style built around their own body and mana. Their strength lies not in raw power, but in technique, eliminating wasted movement,.and inhuman reaction speed.

docs.title: Rogue
docs.text:
A Rogue's mana does not gather strongly in any single part of the body. It spreads thinly and evenly through flesh, bone, nerves, and senses, making their presence unusually difficult to detect.

Because their mana is distributed everywhere, Rogues can redirect it wherever needed: speed, strength, precision, perception, or movement. They rarely surpass specialists in any one area, but their strength lies in adaptability.

More unusually, their mana leaves almost no lasting trace. Physical reinforcement, heightened senses, or mana-enhanced attacks fade without the lingering residue normally left by other Praedari. Even while present, a Rogue may appear as ordinary people to mana perception. They are valued not for overwhelming power, but for subtlety and stealth.

A well-developed Rogue eventually finds strength within their seemingly scattered talents. Some learn to brew poisons for which no cure exists. Others perfect the art of disguise until even magic struggles to see through it.

The path of the Rogue has no single direction, and no one can say with certainty where its limits lie.

docs.title: Martial Artist
docs.text:
Martial artist foundation lies in balance, speed, and precision rather than raw power. They distributes mana through seven connected points running from the base of the spine to the crown of the head. Their discipline is built around keeping these points balanced and allowing mana to flow continuously through the body.

Through constant training in breath, movement, perception, and control, the body begins to act as a single coordinated whole. This gives Martial Artists exceptional speed, balance, agility, and mobility.

They also learn to perceive subtle weaknesses in the body and its mana flow. Rather than relying on overwhelming force, they use precise strikes to disrupt movement, breathing, balance, or mana pathways.

The fortunate few among martial artists may one day discover a true balance within themselves, drawing from all they have practiced without remaining bound to any single form. What emerges from that balance is an art uniquely their own, one that no other person could perform in quite the same way.

docs.title: Paladin
docs.text:
A Paladin is unusual because most are not born Praedari. Their mana awakens later in life when they develop a devotion so absolute that something becomes more important to them than their own survival. Their devotion does not need to belong to a god. It may be directed toward a person, duty, homeland, belief, or cause. What matters is that the devotion is genuine.

A Paladin's mana gathers primarily around the heart and dantian, where it reinforces the body and can be released through a weapon at the moment of impact, producing the devastating strike known as a Smite. As their devotion grows, their mana can also extend to those around them, strengthening and protecting the people they have chosen to defend.

Every Paladin eventually discovers a personal Oath born from that devotion. Breaking it does not remove their power, but turns them into an Oathbreaker, condemned to continuous physical and mental torment forever until they draw their last breath.

Paladins are the rarest known Praedari, and neither training nor talent can reliably create one.

docs.title: Cleric
docs.text:
A Cleric gains divine power because their devotion has been answered by a god. Unlike a Paladin, the power does not become their own. A Cleric remains connected to the deity, allowing divine mana to pass through them when called upon.

Their magic therefore originates from the god rather than the Cleric, and any mana residue left behind carries the identity of that deity.

A Cleric's strength lies in devotion and an ongoing connection to the divine.

docs.title: Warlock
docs.text:
A Warlock gains divine power through a contract with a god. Something is offered, something is demanded, and if both sides agree, the Warlock is allowed to channel that deity's mana. Devotion is not required; the relationship exists because of the bargain.

Like a Cleric, their magic originates from the god rather than themselves, and the mana they leave behind carries the deity's identity.

A Warlock's strength lies in the terms of the pact and the divine power granted through it.

docs.title: Mana Deviation
docs.text:
Mana Deviation occurs when the mana cultivated within a Praedari falls out of its proper pattern and begins moving chaotically through the body. It is usually caused by improper training, forced cultivation, or attempting techniques beyond one's understanding or control.

Instead of reinforcing the body, the unstable mana begins interfering with it and damaging the pathways that normally contain it. The consequences can be severe. Survivors may suffer permanent disabilities or completely lose their ability to use mana.

In the worst cases, the body can no longer withstand the disruption, and Death shall follow.

docs.title: The Races of Avara
docs.text:
Avara is home to eight major races: Humans, Elves, Dwarves, Orcs, Halflings, Goliaths, Half-Elves, and Half-Orcs.

Together, they number more than a billion across the continent, though the true population remains uncertain because the number of Orcs living beyond the borders of organized states has never been reliably counted.

They are not divided neatly into eight civilizations. Humans alone possess countless kingdoms and cultures, while Goliaths are scattered across the continent and Orcs live largely among independent tribes. Elves and Dwarves maintain civilizations of their own, Halflings favor smaller communities, and Half-Elves and Half-Orcs have their own histories shaped by others.

docs.title: The World of Avara
docs.text: A continent divided.Enter the world ↓ The world chronicle

docs.title: A Continent of Many Powers
docs.text:
Avara is a vast continent of rival kingdoms, distinct races, and unfinished disputes. Race and blood remain among the deepest wedges dividing one person from another. Never in its history has the continent known a single unified realm. Many have tried to create one, all have failed.

Human kingdoms, elven states, dwarven holds, and orc tribes have risen across the land only to fall in turn. Borders shift constantly. Old rulers are cast down, and new ones rise to inherit the same ambitions left behind by those who came before them. Five generations may be long enough for a kingdom to disappear, yet it is never enough for transgression to be forgiven.

Thousands of thrones harbor ambitions to rule the land. Treaties may quiet a border for a time, but they cannot erase the past. Every race remembers what was taken from them, and grief has always found a way to linger in the minds of the living long after those who first suffered it are gone.

Every ruler inherits a map covered in unfinished ambitions. Each believes they stand on the right side of history. Many claim they can hear the land itself yearning to be united beneath a single banner. At night, when they finally close their eyes, they dream of glory, prestige, conquest, and the immortality promised to those whose names survive long after their bodies have returned to the earth.

Yet beneath those glorious dreams lies something else.

Fear.

It follows those who wear the crowns quietly, patiently, and persistently. Across generations, it has whispered the same warning into the minds of rulers: If you do not draw first blood, then you will be the one who bleeds.

And so millions of soldiers march across Avara.

They march beneath banners bearing the names of rulers and Gods. One soldier kills for glory and pride, while beside him another drags a civilian by the hair, seeking to satisfy an anger inherited from his long dead ancestors. Others kill in the names of their Gods, offering lives as tribute to the divine. Some march for land, others for vengeance, and many simply because someone above them gave the order.

In the end, the reason matters little to those caught beneath it. Whatever banners are raised and whatever claims of legitimacy are spoken, it is the innocent who are so often made to pay the price.

The fate of the conquered rests entirely upon the whims of the victorious. Across Avara, countless people have questioned the heavens as they drew their final breath, searching for some meaning behind the fate that had befallen them. Those who survive may discover that survival offers little mercy of its own. Throughout the continent can be found eyes that have lost the flicker of hope, belonging to men and women forced to walk in chains while someone behind them carries a whip.

This is Avara.

A continent of poeples united beneath their own banners and divided against everyone who stands beyond them. Yet when every hope of lasting peace seems spent, one Empire looks upon this endless division and sees something greater than ambition.

It sees a responsibility owed to the land.

Avara must be united beneath one law, one crown, and a single throne standing above all others. So the armies of the Empire march, and the kingdoms in their path prepare for the invasion. Walls are strengthened. Armies are assembled. Roads are watched for the first sight of Imperial banners.

When those banners finally appear, many defenders are confronted by something they did not expect.

Imperial standards are carried upright by soldiers trained for war since their teenage years. The sound of the approaching army reaches the walls before individual faces become clear. Thousands of boots striking the road with an almost unnatural unity. Humans, elves, dwarves, halflings, Goliaths, Half Orcs, and Half Elves march beside one another beneath the same banners, preparing to conquer kingdoms whose rulers once believed such unity impossible.

To many rulers beyond its borders, the Empire is an abomination, a manifestation of everything wrong with the world. Its machines challenge what others once believed to be the limits of nature. Its scholars take whatever knowledge proves useful, improve it where they can, and eventually speak of it as part of Imperial civilization. Traditions that endured for thousands of years are erased the moment the Empire decides they have no place in the future it intends to build.

The Empire has looked upon the vast land stretching before it. The continent has been measured, and it has been weighed. To bring Avara beneath a single order and guide it toward its first true age of peace is a responsibility the Empire believes only it alone can bear.

Many call it arrogance.

The Empire calls it destiny.

docs.title: The Mountain Blood
docs.text:
Goliaths originated in the mountains, and much of that ancestry remains visible even among families that have lived elsewhere for generations. Roughly one in five Goliaths is mana-attuned. Their bodies are naturally suited to cold weather, thin air, steep terrain, and long climbs, allowing them to endure conditions that would exhaust most other peoples. Centuries of migration have changed this somewhat, however, and not every modern Goliath is equally comfortable in the mountains.

Without significant mana cultivation, a Goliath can live for around two hundred and twenty years. They reproduce more slowly than humans, though still faster than elves, and commonly stand around seven feet tall, towering over most other peoples of Avara.

Despite their long lives and physical strength, Goliaths are among the rarest peoples on the continent. Their scarcity has less to do with low numbers than with how widely those numbers are spread. Goliath families rarely remain concentrated in one place for many generations. A family may settle somewhere for decades, perhaps even longer, but eventually sons and daughters begin leaving to find their own paths.

Goliaths can be found almost anywhere in Avara, but rarely in great numbers.

docs.title: The Wandering People
docs.text:
There is no sacred pilgrimage that sends Goliaths into the world, nor any traditional age at which they are expected to leave home. Their reasons for wandering can be important or completely trivial. Beneath them all, however, lies the same old curiosity about what might exist beyond the horizon.

A hunter may cross an ocean after hearing stories of a beast they have never seen. A craftsman may travel for years simply to study a foreign technique. Another Goliath may leave because someone once described a distant city badly enough that they decide they must see it for themselves. Their wandering is rarely aimless to them, curiosity is reason enough.

Traditional Goliath communities are usually gatherings of families rather than formal tribes. Related families, close friends, and old companions may remain together for generations, but permanent chiefs and hereditary rulers are uncommon. Leadership tends to exist only when circumstances require it, and authority rarely survives simply because someone's parents once possessed it.

Many disputes in traditional Goliath society have ultimately been resolved in a very Goliath fashion: one person decides there is a large world beyond the argument and leaves to see more of it.

docs.title: Honor and Competition
docs.text:
Goliath culture places enormous importance on honor, honesty, and demonstrated ability. A promise given should be kept, and a fair defeat should be accepted without excuses. Claiming expertise while refusing to prove it brings embarrassment, while cheating in a contest whose rules were agreed upon beforehand is considered deeply dishonorable.

Competition is therefore common among Goliaths. Craftsmanship, medicine, music, storytelling, hunting, navigation, cooking, and countless other pursuits can become fields in which a Goliath seeks mastery.

What matters is not what someone is good at, but whether they have truly earned the right to call themselves good at it.

A physically weak Goliath who becomes a brilliant physician may command far greater respect than a powerful warrior who has accomplished nothing beyond being born strong.

docs.title: Tattoos and Reputation
docs.text:
Traditional Goliath tattoos often record important achievements from the bearer's life: great hunts, mastercrafted works, journeys completed, contests won, or other deeds the individual considers worthy of remembrance. On an older Goliath, the body can become something close to a biography written across the skin.

To outsiders, these tattoos may appear to be little more than elaborate patterns and unfamiliar symbols. To a Goliath who understands them, they can tell the story of a person's life: what they attempted, what they accomplished, and what they believed was worth carrying with them forever.

Because of this, falsely claiming an achievement through a tattoo is considered an especially serious disgrace. Such a mark is not merely dishonest decoration. It is a lie deliberately carved into the body and displayed openly before anyone who knows how to read it.

For a Goliath who chooses to carry such a lie, the punishment is death.

docs.title: Language and Faith
docs.text:
Centuries of migration have produced many Goliath dialects, sometimes different enough that two distant communities may initially struggle to understand one another. All of them, however, descend from the same older tongue, and common roots remain recognizable. Given enough time together, Goliaths from distant parts of Avara can usually become accustomed to one another's speech.

This shared ancestry shapes how they often regard unfamiliar Goliaths. A stranger from the other side of the continent may still be treated much like a distant cousin whose family simply took a different road centuries ago.

Traditional Goliath culture is not strongly religious. Individual Goliaths may become deeply faithful, especially those who settle among other peoples, but historically their communities have placed little authority in temples, priesthoods, or religious institutions. Faith is neither forbidden nor mocked. It simply occupies a less central place than it does in many other cultures.

Their attention tends to settle more naturally upon things that can be experienced, tested, accomplished, or proven.

docs.title: Goliaths and Other Peoples
docs.text:
Goliaths frequently live among other peoples and often become part of foreign settlements, armies, workshops, merchant communities, or families of close companions. Romantic relationships outside their own people nevertheless remain uncommon, and no reliably documented mixed Goliath offspring are known.

Most scholars therefore believe that Goliaths cannot reproduce with other peoples, though the evidence remains limited. With Goliaths scattered so widely across Avara and their numbers already small, certainty has proven difficult to obtain.

Goliath slaves are similarly rare. A Goliath may understand defeat and accept that losing has consequences. They may endure imprisonment, punishment, ransom, or even voluntary service to someone who defeated them fairly. What they generally reject is the belief that defeat gives another person permanent ownership over their body, choices, and future.

For many Goliaths, bondage crosses a line that defeat does not. Many have chosen death rather than permanent slavery.

docs.title: The Measure of a Goliath
docs.text:
Goliaths possess no shared empire, king, homeland, or single unified language. Centuries of wandering have scattered them across Avara until two Goliaths born thousands of miles apart may share little beyond distant ancestry and a handful of recognizable customs.

Yet certain values survived the distance.

A Goliath is expected to stand behind what they claim. A promise should be kept. A defeat honestly earned should be accepted. Achievement must be proven rather than declared, and reputation should be built from deeds rather than inheritance.

Life is too large to spend entirely in one place and when it puts something before you that is truly worthy of your attention, do not hesitate.

Run towards it.

docs.title: The Unwanted Future
docs.text:
Half-orcs and half-elves are treated with prejudice and disdain across much of Avara. In many places, they are seen less as people and more as objects, curiosities, or reminders of something others would rather forget. For them, even receiving basic decency can become a struggle.

There is only one place where half-orcs and half-elves are welcomed openly, without persecution or prejudice, but that is another story. This Codex concerns only how their lineages began. Be warned, these are not tales of forbidden love or innocent infatuation.

For half-elves, the story begins with a darker desire shared between humans and elves.

docs.title: Half-Elves
docs.text:
Half-elves closely resemble pure-blooded elves, enough that the difference may not be obvious at first glance. The clearest distinctions are their shorter lifespans and lower rate of mana attunement compared to full-blooded elves. Humans sometimes claim they can recognize a half-elf by the way they carry themselves, as they rarely possess the unmistakable pride associated with pure-blooded elves. Elves have another way of knowing. Those sensitive to mana can feel the difference in the weaker quality that surrounds a half-elf.

Human fascination with elven beauty is hardly a secret. Many humans would never openly admit how deeply elves captivate them, but their eyes often reveal enough. Among elves, humans hold a peculiar place as well. Many elves regard humans as lesser versions of themselves, similar enough to be interesting but inferior enough not to be considered equals. Some elves have even kept humans as pets or curiosities simply out of fascination.

From this unhealthy fascination came many half-elven bloodlines.

Almost every half-elf lineage begins with the child of a human and a pure-blooded elf, and the circumstances behind those unions are rarely pleasant. Elven slaves are highly valued among humans, particularly those captured as spoils of war and prized for their appearance. Their beauty turns them into commodities, and many are treated more like possessions than living people.

The elven side is no kinder. Humans have also been kept and used as objects through which elves indulge desires they would never openly acknowledge. Male human slaves are especially sought after in certain Dark Elf societies, where fascination with humans can take forms just as cruel as those found among human slaveholders.

The children born from these relationships are often unwanted by both sides. Humans may look upon half-elves with the same fascination they hold toward elves themselves, treating them as desirable for a time before discarding them when that fascination fades. Elves often see something more shameful: a living reminder of desires they would rather keep hidden. The fact that half-elves possess shorter lives and weaker mana than pure-blooded elves only deepens that contempt.

For many half-elves, the prejudice begins the moment they are born. Some are treated as possessions, while others are ignored entirely. Wherever they go, they may find themselves judged not for anything they have done, but simply for what their existence represents to others.

As unjust as the lives of half-elves can be, their counterparts are often treated even more harshly.

docs.title: Half-Orcs
docs.text:
If the history of half-elves begins with dark fascination and desire, the history of half-orcs often begins with one word:

Captives.

Orc tribes are infamous throughout Avara for warfare, raiding, and their unusually high fertility. Many cities and settlements have fallen to orc raids over the centuries, and when those raids succeed, captives are often carried away unwillingly.

Orc tribes can rise with frightening speed, but they can be destroyed just as quickly. When other armies eventually break those tribes and reclaim what was lost, they sometimes find something few wish to confront among the survivors: women carrying orc children.

What follows is rarely merciful.

Some mothers are killed while the half-orc child is still inside the womb. Others are allowed to give birth before the child is killed afterward. Only a fortunate few are given any chance at life. Some mothers escape and disappear into secluded places where neither their former captors nor their own people can easily find them. Some half-orc children are abandoned. Others survive only to be sold into slavery later.

Those who reach adulthood often carry their orcish blood visibly. Half-orcs tend to develop powerful musculature, and their tusks remain clearly formed even though they are smaller than those of a full-blooded orc. Many also have a reputation for being quick-tempered and easy to anger.

Whether an individual half-orc deserves that reputation often matters very little.

To many civilizations, the first thing they see when they look at a half-orc is the ancestor behind them. The barbarian. The raider. The warmonger. The orc who once burned settlements and carried away captives. A half-orc may have committed none of those crimes, yet they are forced to carry the hatred left behind by those who did.

Because of this, many half-orcs find themselves living as mercenaries or slaves, with very little between the two. Their lives are shaped by persecution for actions they never committed, and many are hated simply for existing.

Even full-blooded orcs offer them little comfort. To many tribes, half-orcs are merely smaller and weaker versions of themselves. In a society where weakness is often despised, there is little reason for the tribe to welcome them.

For much of history, half-orcs moved constantly from one place to another. In that sense, their lives sometimes resembled those of the goliaths, who were likewise scattered across Avara rather than gathered into large settled civilizations.

The difference is that goliaths wandered because it was part of their way of life.

Half-orcs wandered because they had to.

To many people in Avara, half-orcs remain the embodiment of a defiled lineage.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Halflings are often considered the strangest civilization in Avara.

While other peoples compete for territory, wealth, influence, and power, halflings are more likely to spend their time deciding what they will have for dinner. There is no known halfling civilization larger than a small city. Unlike many other races, halflings have little interest in building great kingdoms or expanding their borders.

Instead, they live in scattered villages, farming communities, and merchant towns.

Halflings have a strong sense of when something is enough. A warm meal, a comfortable home, good company, and honest work are enough to make many of them content. Other races sometimes mistake this attitude for laziness, but halflings do believe in hard work.

They simply believe that enjoying the present is just as important as preparing for the future.

docs.title: The Halfling Body
docs.text:
Halflings are small humanoids, usually standing around three feet tall. Their bodies are compact, but their proportions remain recognizably adult despite their height.

Halflings age very slowly in appearance, although their actual lifespans are similar to those of humans. Because of this, judging a halfling's age by appearance alone is extremely difficult. A middle-aged halfling may look remarkably young, sometimes resembling someone who has not yet reached adulthood.

Halflings are also naturally nimble and dexterous. They can climb, crawl, squeeze, and reach places that larger people would struggle to enter.

Combined with their youthful appearance and easygoing behavior, a group of adult halflings working in a field may easily be mistaken for children playing among the crops.

docs.title: Uncanny Luck
docs.text:
Halflings are absurdly lucky.

No scholar has found a convincing explanation for how or why this happens, but there is no shortage of examples. A halfling might accidentally wander into the path of a stampede, only to be found afterward without so much as a bruise. An arrow aimed directly at a halfling's head might miss because, at that exact moment, the halfling crouched down to pick up a silver coin lying in the dirt.

Halflings themselves rarely consider these events unusual. Ask one how they survived something that should have killed them, and the answer is often little more than:

“I don't know.”

Then they go home and start preparing dinner.

docs.title: Tribes and Communities
docs.text:
Halflings have historically lived in small, loosely organized communities rather than powerful states. Their villages and small cities usually govern themselves according to whatever arrangement keeps daily life running smoothly, arguments reasonably short, and dinner more or less on time.

Leadership is practical rather than ceremonial. Someone trusted by the community may speak on behalf of everyone else, but formal institutions usually appear only when they become necessary.

This has occasionally caused problems for foreign diplomats. A diplomat might arrive in a halfling settlement and ask to speak with its ruler. The halflings will usually discuss the matter among themselves for a while before returning with another question:

“What is a ruler?”

docs.title: Fear and Violence
docs.text:
The exact rate of mana attunement among halflings is unknown, though the closest estimate is around one in ten. The lack of reliable information has a simple explanation: many halfling Praedari do not live like Praedari at all.

A halfling capable of becoming a powerful warrior or mage may instead choose to spend their life farming, trading, raising a family, or practicing some ordinary craft. For them, a productive day followed by a warm meal at home may be more appealing than fame or power.

This easygoing nature sometimes causes outsiders to believe halflings are easy to exploit. Few assumptions about halflings are more dangerous.

When faced with danger, halflings can become remarkably calm and calculating. Their bravery is different from the reckless charge of an orc or the stubborn willingness of a goliath to fight for honor until death.

Halfling courage is practical, they observe the situation, measure the risks, consider their chances, and act accordingly. Their small size already makes them difficult targets. Their natural agility makes them harder to catch. Add their uncanny luck, and dealing with a determined group of halflings can become a miserable experience very quickly.

Halfling settlements may be small, they may appear poorly defended, they may even look harmless. Those who try to conquer one usually discover that the trouble involved is far greater than anything they expected to gain.

docs.title: The Vassals
docs.text:
Many great kingdoms prefer to deal with halfling communities through carefully negotiated agreements involving taxes, levies, protection, and vassalage. In exchange for cooperation, halfling settlements often receive military protection, roads, infrastructure, and access to the wider economy. As a result, many halfling villages and cities exist under the patronage of larger kingdoms while continuing to manage most of their own affairs.

Humans, elves, and dwarves tend to agree on one thing when dealing with halflings:

The best way to profit from them is through a clear agreement of give and take. Halflings are known for taking agreements seriously. They will not give more than what was promised, but they will not give less either.

If a halfling village agrees to pay a certain amount of tax, the payment will arrive when it is supposed to, down to the last coin. For this reason, halfling communities are often considered reliable investments by the kingdoms that protect them. They will rarely provide endless wealth or fuel great ambitions. But they are stable and when the tax collector arrives, the gold will be there.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
There is no single human civilization.

Human kingdoms differ in nearly every way imaginable. One may be ruled by a hereditary monarch, another by an elected assembly, and a third by institutions that would be unrecognizable to either. Their customs, laws, values, and political traditions can change dramatically within only a few generations.

Human societies rarely remain unchanged for long. Five human kingdoms may stand beside one another and still produce five entirely different cultures.

docs.title: The Human Body
docs.text:
Humans possess few extreme natural advantages. They are neither especially large nor small, neither naturally strong nor particularly frail, and their physical traits vary greatly between populations. Roughly one in twenty humans is capable of becoming a Praedari.

Most humans live between seventy and ninety years, though some reach a century. Powerful Praedari can live considerably longer, depending on how far their mana cultivation develops.

Compared with many other peoples of Avara, the human body is remarkably ordinary. Yet that has never stopped humanity from becoming the most populous people on the continent.

docs.title: The Middle Ground
docs.text:
Humans are competent in almost everything, yet they rarely possess the natural gifts other peoples are born with. They do not have the strength of Goliaths, the longevity of elves, the uncanny fortune of halflings, or many of the other traits that distinguish the peoples of Avara.

Humanity is well aware of this.

That awareness has shaped them for generations. Humans train where others rely on instinct, study what others inherit naturally, and borrow whatever techniques proven useful. What they lack in natural specialization, they often compensate for through effort, imitation, and a strong sense of pragmatism.

If another race possesses an advantage humanity does not, humans rarely spend long mourning the difference. They learn from it and take what they can. All in the name of survival, and perhaps one day to thrive as the pioneers of Avara.

docs.title: Adaptability
docs.text:
Humanity's greatest natural strength is adaptability.

Humans can settle across almost every region of Avara, and over generations their societies reshape themselves around the places they inhabit. A kingdom built along great rivers will develop differently from one surrounded by mountains. A wealthy trading state will think differently from a nation trapped between stronger neighbors. Geography, enemies, resources, and opportunity all leave their mark.

Humanity therefore possesses no single fixed way of life. They adapt until their culture fits the world around them, and when that world changes, they change with it.

This ability can make human societies difficult to define from the outside. Customs considered sacred in one century may be abandoned in the next, while ideas borrowed from former enemies can eventually become traditions defended as though they had always existed.

For humans, survival has rarely required remaining the same.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
Humanity's greatest practical advantage is its population.

Their fertility, combined with their ability to settle a wide range of environments, has allowed humans to spread across much of Avara. Even where individual human kingdoms rise and fall, humanity itself remains difficult to dislodge.

Large populations provide obvious advantages: more soldiers, more workers, more craftsmen, more scholars, and more people capable of filling whatever role a society requires. But numbers provide humanity with something else as well.

More chances.

Humans do not need every person among them to be extraordinary. They can produce millions of ordinary people and wait for the rare individual who is not. A brilliant commander, a powerful Praedari, or a scholar who discovers something no one before them understood.

Humanity needs only one such person to emerge among millions, and once they do, there are millions others following what that person begins.

docs.title: Human Alliances
docs.text:
Human kingdoms frequently form alliances with one another, and this too can be seen as another expression of their adaptability. Humans are often willing to cooperate when cooperation offers the better chance of survival.

Such alliances are rarely permanent.

Two kingdoms that spent generations fighting over a border may suddenly stand together when a greater threat appears. Old insults are set aside, treaties are signed, armies march beneath neighboring banners, and rulers who once despised one another discover reasons to speak politely.

Once the threat disappears, however, both kingdoms may soon return to aiming at each other's throats. Human alliances are often built less upon affection than necessity, but necessity has proven more than enough to unite them when circumstances demand it.

docs.title: The Human Contradiction
docs.text:
Humans live beside races who often seem naturally better suited to particular tasks, yet humanity can be found almost everywhere in Avara.

Human kingdoms collapse and new ones rise from their remains. Conquered peoples adopt the methods of their conquerors, then reshape those methods into something of their own. Foreign disciplines become local traditions. Cities destroyed by war are rebuilt, sometimes by the grandchildren of those who watched them burn.

Humanity possesses no single ideal form it must preserve, and that is both its strength and its weakness. Humans change quickly, governments, religions, customs, military traditions, and even entire identities can transform within a handful of generations.

Other races may look upon that constant change as instability. Humans often call it survival. They are rarely the people naturally best suited to whatever must be done.

But they are remarkably good at becoming what the world demands.
